Respiratory trials conducted on resting specimens of the Checkerboard worm lizard (Trogonophis wiegmanni) under controlled laboratory conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 0.0032 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 0.0032 milliliters of oxygen per minute], placing this species among the most energetically conservative members of the family Trogonophidae. This exceptionally low oxygen consumption, likely an adaptation to the species' fossorial existence, reflects the reduced energetic demands of a life spent within burrow systems in the sandy soils of northwest Africa. When compared to other amphisbaenians, this metabolic rate sits at the lower end of the known range, a distinction that may be tied to the checkerboard worm lizard's relatively modest body dimensions. Females in particular exhibit a modest ultimate wet weight, with fully grown adults reaching approximately 19.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 19.6 grams], a state often associated with a total length of around 25 centimeters and a cylindrical body width of about 1 centimeter. This robust yet slender form facilitates efficient subsurface locomotion while imposing constraints on overall mass accumulation, which in turn influences energy allocation patterns across the lifetime of these secretive reptiles.


The species shows a distinct life-history trajectory that reflects its fossorial habits and seasonal environmental constraints. Under incubation temperatures maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], embryos complete their development over a period of approximately 90 days [ab = approximately 90 days], a duration that appears intimately tied to thermal conditions within the subterranean nest chamber. Upon hatching, neonates emerge at a wet weight of 0.7 grams [Wwb = 0.7 grams], a remarkably low initial mass that nonetheless contains sufficient yolk reserves to sustain the young during their first few days of independent life before they commence active foraging on soil invertebrates. The age at birth is thus closely linked to the thermal profile of the nesting environment, with slight deviations in temperature likely accelerating or extending the incubation interval in ways that could affect hatchling viability and subsequent growth performance. Comparative data from related amphisbaenian species suggest that such extended incubation periods are not uncommon among fossorial squamates, possibly serving to delay emergence until favorable soil moisture or prey availability conditions are met.


For females of the Checkerboard worm lizard, the transition to reproductive competence follows a notably protracted timeline, particularly when assessed under a stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Capture-mark-recapture studies and dissection of ovarian tissue have demonstrated that the time since metamorphosis at puberty for females is approximately 1,095 days since metamorphosis [tp = approximately 1,095 days since metamorphosis], or roughly three years, based on extrapolations from the better-studied congener Am at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]phisbaena alba. This extended pre-reproductive phase, during which females must accumulate sufficient body reserves and attain a body size close to the ultimate wet weight of 19.6 grams [Wwi = 19.6 grams], suggests that reproductive onset is constrained more by energetic thresholds than by chronological age alone. The delay may reflect the slow growth rates typical of many fossorial species, where the energetic cost of burrowing and the unpredictability of subsurface food resources limit the rate at which individuals can channel resources into somatic development. It remains unclear whether males follow a similar pattern, as the current estimates are derived specifically from female datasets.


Reproductive output in Trogonophis wiegmanni is characterized by a modest but consistent investment per season. At a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce a single clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs per year], with each clutch containing exactly 8 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing exactly 8 eggs]. This reproductive schedule, which yields a total annual output of 8 eggs per year, places the species at the lower end of lizard fecundity even among amphisbaenians, a pattern likely driven by the physical constraints of burrow-nesting and the limited space available for clutch accommodation within the narrow body cavity. The combination of small clutch size and low annual frequency underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival over high fecundity, possibly because each egg must contain enough yolk to support an extended incubation period of roughly 90 days [ab = roughly 90 days] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Field observations suggest that the leathery-shelled eggs are deposited in a single chamber within the parent's burrow system, where they receive no further parental care.


Longevity records for the Checkerboard worm lizard, estimated from patterns observed in the related species Amphisbaena alba and corroborated by sporadic recapture data, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5,475 days [am = approximately 5,475 days], or 15 years, when maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with a late onset of reproduction at about three years of age, reinforces the interpretation of a slow life-history strategy that is common among burrowing squamates. In captive settings, individuals have been documented to persist into their sixteenth year, though such prolonged survival may outpace what is achievable under natural conditions where predation, resource limitation, and thermal extremes impose additional mortality pressures. The basal metabolic rate of 0.0032 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 0.0032 milliliters of oxygen per minute] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] suggests that low daily energetic expenditures contribute to this extended lifespan by reducing the cumulative oxidative damage typically associated with higher metabolic demands. The species' capacity to endure periods of food scarcity further supports this model of a slow-paced existence, with individuals emerging from winter dormancy in good condition despite months without feeding.
